newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Lights go back on in Marcos mausoleum.
newsitem.headline: Lights go back on in Marcos mausoleum.

text.p: The crypt holding the preserved corpse of former Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos glowed again on Thursday after three days of darkness because of unpaid electricity bills.
Using a second-hand generator, Mayor Jesus Nalupta restored power in the air-conditioned tomb in Marcos's home town of Batac town but he said he was not sure how long the generator would last.
"We bought it in 1990 from a store selling second-hand equipment from Japan. Maybe it is 10 or 20 years old," Nalupta said.
A local electric cooperative on Monday shut down power in the Marcos family compound where the mausoleum stands after the family failed to settle bills totalling 5.6 million pesos ($214,500).
In Manila, former first lady Imelda Marcos raged at President Fidel Ramos's refusal to allow the former ruler to be buried at the Heroes Cemetery in the capital.
"President Ramos cannot change history, that Marcos was a soldier," Mrs Marcos said, referring to her late husband's exploits in World War Two.
Ramos, now visiting south Asia, said on Tuesday the Marcoses were free to bury the former president anywhere in Manila except at the Heroes Cemetery, which required presidential approval.

"If he will not allow that, it is as if we are back to the law of the jungles, where might is right... We will just wait until we can give him an honourable burial," she told Reuters in her luxurious high-rise apartment.
"I will have the patience of Job," she added. Job is a biblical figure who endured untold sufferings but was rewarded by God in the end.

Asked how she could afford to live in an apartment adorned with works of art, including a painting by Picasso and a sculpture by Michelangelo, and yet not pay the electricity bills, Marcos broke into tears.
She said the government had taken away everything she owned and what she now had came from friends.
"We would have paid it (the bills) if they had not sequestered everything," she said.
The government has accused the Marcoses of looting up to $5 billion from the economy during their 20-year rule and taken custody of their known assets pending a court ruling on their ownership.

Marcos was ousted in a popular revolt in 1986 and died in exile in Hawaii three years later. Ramos, his cousin, allowed his remains to be brought to Batac in 1993 but refused to allow a burial in Manila, fearing it would provoke violence.
Preserved with chemicals, the wax-like corpse lies in an elevated glass coffin, bathed in soft lights while classical music plays in the background.
Until Monday, hundreds of tourists and Marcos's own townmates regularly flocked to the place to view the corpse.
"Bury Marcos, cremate him but never put the dictator with our heroes," Max Soliven, veteran political columnist and publisher, said in his column in the Philippine Star newspaper.

"Why elevate the late Marcos to the level of our bayani (hero)? Bury him and have done with it -- somewhere else," Soliven added, warning unless this was done, "we shall see tyranny someday raising its monstrous head again."
